meta.title: The Pragmatic Maxim
meta.subtitle: Meaning is the conceivable practical bearings of a conception

report_card.summary: Charles Sanders Peirce's pragmatic maxim is a rule of logic, not a theory of truth: the meaning of an intellectual conception is the whole of the conceivable effects that would have practical bearings. Grade-one familiarity and grade-two definition are incomplete until those bearings are specified. William James popularized 'pragmatism' from 1898 in a more sensational key; Peirce coined 'pragmaticism' in 1905 to fence the original maxim. Later formulations locate meaning in the conditional, self-controlled conduct of interpreters rather than in any finite list of observed upshots.

key_stats.label: Illustrations of the Logic of Science papers

story.title: A Maxim, Not a Mood
story.narration: The pragmatic maxim is a rule for the third grade of clearness, stated by Charles Sanders Peirce in 1878. Consider the conceivable effects with practical bearings; that conception of effects is the whole conception of the object. It is a maxim of logic aimed at inquiry, not a temperament and not a slogan that truth is whatever works.

story.title: Two Grades Are Not Enough
story.narration: Familiarity with a word and a crisp verbal definition are Descartes' clear-and-distinct pair, recycled as Peirce's first two grades. They still leave disputes standing. The third grade asks what difference the conception would make to informed practice. Without that question, clarity is only typographic.

story.title: Thought Is for Habits
story.narration: In How to Make Our Ideas Clear, Peirce writes that the whole function of thought is to produce habits of action. Meaning is not a private picture. To develop a conception, determine the habits it involves — the general ways an interpreter would be prepared to act if the conception were true.

story.title: Laboratory Logic, 1877–78
story.narration: The maxim is the second paper in Illustrations of the Logic of Science, published in Popular Science Monthly. The Fixation of Belief (November 1877) defends the scientific method of settling belief against tenacity, authority, and a priori taste. How to Make Our Ideas Clear (January 1878) then supplies the matching account of meaning. Peirce is writing as a Coast Survey scientist, not as a metaphysician shopping for a school.

story.title: James Takes It Public
story.narration: William James prints the word pragmatism in 1898, crediting Peirce and the early-1870s Metaphysical Club, where Chauncey Wright had already demanded a fallibilist empiricism. James's later Lowell lectures recast the maxim around sensations to expect and reactions to prepare. John Dewey carries the movement into education and democratic inquiry. The brand now travels farther than the 1878 laboratory rule.

story.title: Ugly Enough to Be Safe
story.narration: By 1905 Peirce judges that popular pragmatism has drifted toward cash-value and temperament. He coins pragmaticism — ugly enough to be safe from kidnappers — to mark a method for clarifying intellectual concepts, not a metaphysics. Empty metaphysics is whatever survives verbal definition but evaporates when asked for conceivable practical bearings.

story.title: Meaning Lives in Interpreter Conduct
story.narration: Peirce restates the maxim across decades; Schmidt catalogues 61 formulations. The 1903 lectures tighten the claim: a theoretical judgment means a practical maxim whose apodosis is imperative. Difference of conception is difference in how, taken with other intentions, it might conceivably modify deliberate, self-controlled conduct. Actual test results are upshots. Meaning is the general habit those upshots would train. That is the climax of the rule: not the object's behavior alone, but the interpreter's prepared conduct.

story.title: Fallibilists Recover the Strict Reading
story.narration: Christopher Hookway and Cheryl Misak read the maxim as a rule of reflective clarity inside a fallibilist account of inquiry, continuous with The Fixation of Belief and hostile to Cartesian foundations. The Collected Papers keep the 1878 text in circulation (CP 5.388–410), but the scholarship insists on the later, stricter formulations rather than James's popular restatement.

story.title: Draw the Effects, or Stay at Grade Two
story.narration: The maxim is itself a visualization instruction. A graph of named philosophers and book titles is only grade two. Grade three is the edge set: what accepting the maxim would change in inquiry, in a dispute, in an interpreter's next action. If two vocabularies license the same conceivable habits, they do not mark two meanings.

insights.title: The pragmatic maxim is a rule of conceptual hygiene, not a theory that truth equals whatever works
insights.body: Peirce offers a method for the third grade of clearness of intellectual concepts. Collapsing the maxim into 'pragmatism means useful' is exactly the drift that forced the 1905 rename. Meaning is specified by conceivable practical bearings; truth remains correspondence to what inquiry would find if pressed far enough.

insights.title: Verbal definition without conceivable effects is how empty metaphysics survives inspection
insights.body: Grades one and two — familiarity and definition — let disputes look substantial while licensing identical conduct. Peirce's purge is operational: if no conceivable practical difference can be traced, the alternatives are not two meanings. The 1902 dictionary entry on pragmatism advertises this as a cleanup of metaphysics.

insights.title: Jamesian popularization and Peircean pragmaticism are one brand that split into two methods
insights.body: James's 1898 print debut and later Lowell lectures recast the maxim around sensations and prepared reactions, which travels. Peirce's 1905 coinage fences a narrower logical method. Treating them as interchangeable erases the only distinction Peirce thought worth an ugly neologism.

insights.title: Meaning attaches to general habits of interpreters, not to any finite list of observed payoffs
insights.body: Because a conception is general, its purport is the implications for general practice. Particular experimental outcomes are upshots, not meanings. The 1903 accent and Schmidt's survey of 61 formulations converge on conditional propositions about self-controlled conduct.

insights.title: The 1877–78 pair is one machine: fixation of belief plus clarification of meaning
insights.body: The Fixation of Belief argues that only the scientific method answers to a reality independent of what a community wishes. How to Make Our Ideas Clear then refuses conceptions that could not make a difference inside that method. Separating the maxim from the inquiry essay turns it into a slogan.

insights.title: A knowledge graph of names without effect-edges has only reached Peirce's second grade of clearness
insights.body: Listing Peirce, James, Dewey, and the 1878 essay is familiarity plus definition. The maxim's own instruction is to encode the bearings: what the rule does to empty metaphysics, to Jamesian pragmatism, and to an interpreter who accepts a conception as clear. Visualization that stops at biography fails the maxim it depicts.

insights.title: Fallibilist scholarship is the live opportunity to keep the maxim operational rather than anthologized
insights.body: Hookway and Misak relocate the maxim inside inquiry, perception, and anti-Cartesian epistemology instead of leaving it as a quotation. That reading makes the maxim usable on contemporary conceptual disputes — including how tools, agents, and knowledge systems claim to 'mean' something by what they change in practice.

clusters.label: Maxim and Grades of Clearness
clusters.description: The logical core: three grades of clearness, conceivable practical effects, habit of action, interpreter conduct, and the empty metaphysics the maxim is designed to dissolve.

clusters.label: Founders and Interlocutors
clusters.description: The people and the early conversation that produced the name pragmatism and later forced Peirce to rename his own doctrine.

clusters.label: 1877–78 Laboratory Texts
clusters.description: The published machine: the six-paper series, the two key essays, the magazine that carried them, and the collected edition that keeps the text in print.

clusters.label: Reformulation Timeline
clusters.description: Dated turns: original statement, James's print debut, the 1903 conduct formulation, and the 1905 pragmaticism fence.

clusters.label: Later Cartography
clusters.description: Scholarship that maps 61 formulations and relocates the maxim inside fallibilist inquiry rather than leaving it as a quotation.

nodes.label: Pragmatic Maxim
nodes.description: Peirce's rule for the third grade of clearness: the meaning of a conception is the conception of its conceivable practical effects.

nodes.label: Charles Sanders Peirce
nodes.description: American logician and scientist (1839–1914) who formulated the maxim in 1878 and later renamed his doctrine pragmaticism.

metrics.survey_years: 32 at U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey

nodes.label: Conceivable Practical Effects
nodes.description: The content the maxim equates with meaning: general bearings on informed practice, not a finite checklist of observed results.

nodes.label: How to Make Our Ideas Clear
nodes.description: January 1878 essay in Popular Science Monthly where the maxim first appears in English, as paper two of Illustrations of the Logic of Science.

nodes.label: Three Grades of Clearness
nodes.description: Peirce's completion of Cartesian clarity: familiarity, distinct definition, and conceivable practical bearings.

nodes.label: Habit of Action
nodes.description: Peirce's claim that the function of thought is to produce habits of action; a conception means the habits it involves.

nodes.label: William James
nodes.description: Psychologist-philosopher who put 'pragmatism' into print in 1898 and restated the maxim around sensations and prepared reactions.

nodes.label: Pragmaticism
nodes.description: Peirce's 1905 rename of his own doctrine, coined to separate a logical method of clarification from popular pragmatism.

nodes.label: Empty Metaphysics
nodes.description: Conceptions that look clear at grades one and two but license no conceivable difference in practice — the target the maxim is built to dissolve.

nodes.label: The Fixation of Belief
nodes.description: November 1877 companion essay arguing that only the scientific method of settling belief answers to a reality independent of wish.

nodes.label: Illustrations of the Logic of Science
nodes.description: Peirce's 1877–78 six-paper series in Popular Science Monthly that houses both the fixation essay and the maxim essay.

nodes.label: Scientific Method of Fixing Belief
nodes.description: The method Peirce contrasts with tenacity, authority, and a priori taste: inquiry that answers to an independent real.

nodes.label: Interpreter Conduct
nodes.description: Later Peircean accent: the meaning of an intellectual concept is a conditional about the deliberate, self-controlled conduct of its interpreters.

nodes.label: John Dewey
nodes.description: Carries pragmatism into education, democracy, and inquiry-as-reconstruction; part of the popular current Peirce distinguished himself from.

nodes.label: Chauncey Wright
nodes.description: Metaphysical Club interlocutor remembered by Peirce and James as demanding a phenomenalist, fallibilist empiricism.

nodes.label: Metaphysical Club
nodes.description: Informal early-1870s Cambridge conversation in which James later said Peirce coined the name pragmatism.

nodes.label: Popular Science Monthly
nodes.description: Magazine that published the 1877–78 Illustrations series, including both key essays.

nodes.label: 1878 Maxim Statement
nodes.description: First English statement of the maxim in How to Make Our Ideas Clear, not yet named as such.

nodes.label: 1898 James Print Debut
nodes.description: James's Philosophical Conceptions and Practical Results puts the word pragmatism into print and credits Peirce.

nodes.label: 1903 Pragmatism Lectures
nodes.description: Peirce's lectures recast theoretical judgments as confused forms of practical maxims with imperative force.

nodes.label: 1905 Pragmaticism Coinage
nodes.description: Peirce publicly renames his doctrine to separate a logical method from the popular movement.

nodes.label: Jon Alan Schmidt
nodes.description: Catalogues 61 formulations of the maxim and argues that ultimate meaning is a conditional about interpreter conduct.

nodes.label: Christopher Hookway
nodes.description: Reads the maxim as a rule of reflective clarity inside Peirce's scientific, fallibilist account of inquiry.

nodes.label: Cheryl Misak
nodes.description: Treats the maxim as leverage on a concept inside a Peircean account of truth, inquiry, and anti-Cartesian epistemology.

nodes.label: Cartesian Clear and Distinct Ideas
nodes.description: The two-grade picture of clarity Peirce inherits and then declares incomplete without practical bearings.

nodes.label: Collected Papers of C. S. Peirce
nodes.description: Standard reprint locus of the 1878 maxim (CP 5.388–410) through which most later readers meet the text.
